text_fidelity_a: Roku 3 Streaming Media Player (2014 model) Without repeating what everyone has said here, I will speak for Roku's support of the Plex media streaming software which is a free Roku channel. If you have never heard of it, it is a fantastic solution that allows you to use Roku (as well as all your portable devices and remote computers, including ones on the internet-at-large) to stream all of the movies on your computer, regardless of the format. On Roku, you can browse the movie collection on your computer using a slick interface and watch it in full resolution. (This is only if you have a fast connection like a home wireless network, and you need to configure it to do this- an easy settings change.) If your computer can play it, so can your Roku. The key to this is because all the transcoding of the video file happens on your computer so all Roku has to do is play the video stream. The result is that you can easily fast-forward and rewind, as well and have the jump-back feature like the TiVo has. This was the primary reason that I bought the Roku as it is a lot easier to use than trying to connect your computer directly to your TV and muddling about with computer controls to watch movies. The Plex interface on Roku is easy to use and very slick. It does nice things like look up movie data so you have the cover art, theme music, and movie info for you to peruse as you are browsing your library. Finally, there is the "Plex it!" feature which you can use with your computer's browser, so that when you find a video on the internet on your computer, you want to queue it up for later to watch on your TV, and it will appear in your movie queue in Plex on Roku, regardless of the video format! This also gets around the one annoying thing about Roku and that it doesn't have a native YouTube channel for some reason.
text_fidelity_b: Roku 3 Streaming Media Player (2014 model)

Jabra STONE Bluetooth Headset with Extreme-Noise Blocking (Discontinued by Manufacturer) Pros:

1. I liked it for its looks at first sight. One of the sleekest looking Bluetooth ear devices that I've ever seen.
2. Almost unnoticeable when nestled in tight, snuggling up to your ear
3. Nice convenient pod for charging and carrying around, looking like a cute little black egg

Cons:

1. Once you can get it to fit comfortably in your ear, it sounds wonderful. Unfortunately, it doesn't fit my ear and due to the placement of the invisible control buttons, every time I try to adjust it, I either disconnect the call or re-dial the last call.
2. It makes me do a LOT of redialling as it keeps slipping out of place.
3. Maybe I was doing something wrong but I couldn't get it to pair with my Blackberry or my iPod.
4. Does not keep the charge for the 8 hours as promised. It discharges very quickly (in a couple of hours, or so it felt) especially when compared to the length of time it takes to re-charge.
5. I couldn't use it on my left ear, which for me, wasn't quite right
6. The art of raising or lowering the volume by sliding a finger along the headset has thus far eluded me.

This device is one you'd buy for looks, but not for life.

Amanda Richards
October 25, 2010
text_fidelity_b: Jabra STONE Bluetooth Headset with Extreme-Noise Blocking (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

If you're reading a 2-3-or-4- book set, and you're ready to move to the next in the series, you must have fewer than 10 loaded. The creators of Kindle and the new Kindle Unlimited seem to just keep coming up with better and better ideas!

text_fidelity_a:
Anker Ergonomic Optical USB Wired Vertical Mouse 1000/1600 DPI, 5 Buttons CE100 It takes some getting used to. I have three of these Anker ergos. Two are wireless and are in use at work. One is wired and on my gaming rig at home.

Gaming: My normal mouse is a Logitech gaming mouse which had been my go to for many years. It was fast accurate and had plenty of built in controls for everything I needed. This mouse also has all of the relevant controls and the resolution button is less likely to get accidentally hit than on the Logitech. It does still get hit here and there though. I also find that the vertical style while more comfortable is not as ideal for gaming but honestly speaking is a small niggle in that the comfort is far more appreciated than the slightly awkward hand position (as movements need to be very fast). Is this up to par with other premium gaming controllers? I have my doubts, but it is certainly comfortable and as a wired controller is adequate for sure.

Everyday: Just yes. Especially considering the value. It is both affordable as an ergonomic mouse and comfortable. You may need to make adjustments to your seating angle as the tendency is for this mouse to be most comfortable when your forearm is almost flat on the desk surface.

Look and feel: It is not an especially heavy mouse. But it does have a level of refinement expected on something more costly. It is also well designed and not obscenely gaudy like a lot of products these days. The rubbery matte surface is pleasant and tactile and the buttons are responsive and easy to actuate. The mouse is somewhat full-sized. I don't want to say large because I have small-medium hands and I can use this just fine, but by no means do I have small hands. Those who have small hands might find this more of a challenge to use though I don't doubt you'll get used to it. The primary buttons and grip would be fine, but the locations of the scroll wheel and the forward nav button are a bit of a reach.

Like I said I have three of these in various formats and love them all. Other than my ultra compact travel mouse, these are used on all of my home and work devices. At such a reasonable cost you can't lose by at least trying it.
text_fidelity_b: Anker Ergonomic Optical USB Wired Vertical Mouse 1000/1600 DPI, 5 Buttons CE100

text_fidelity_a:
Wi4You Recessed Wall Plate 2 Pack Decotive Cable Wall Plate with Fly Mounting Wings Bottom Opening for Low Voltage Cable Pass Through WI1009-2 I wanted a single-gang wall box so I could route pre-terminated Cat6 cables from behind my TV stand to my router in another room. Tired of the glitches you inherently get with wifi when running a FireTV stick 4K with a FireTV Recast so converted all to hardwired ethernet. System is much more responsive now and this product fit the bill. Comes in a 2 pack (one for each end), not expensive, easy to install, and comes with both the wall insert and a trim cover plate. Large opening at bottom inside the wall accommodates both Cat6 plug pass-thru, and multiple cables.

One note of caution: You obviously slide your plugs/cables through the box opening, then insert box into your wall cut-out, then tighten the 2 front screws which cause the flanges inside to flip around and clamp to the back side of your wall board. When tightening the bottom one, be sure none of your cables are trapped between the flange and wall. If so, you could pinch one or more cables.
text_fidelity_b: Wi4You Recessed Wall Plate 2 Pack Decotive Cable Wall Plate with Fly Mounting Wings Bottom Opening for Low Voltage Cable Pass Through WI1009-2

text_fidelity_a:
Soundcore by Anker Life P3 Noise Cancelling Earbuds, Ultra Long 50H Playtime, Fast Charging, Big Bass, Multi-Mode Noise Cancelling, AI-Enhanced Calls, Wireless Charging, App Control, Bluetooth 5.2 Pros: What I said above plus....the sound is even better than most earbuds that cost more than this. The bass could be too thick for some but you can tweak it with equalizer in app if need be. I also like the earbuds turn on automatically when put up against your ear. At least that's what I think is happening. :D It's also nice that the charging case/base has a 3 LED gauge for base battery status and charging status. So a full charge with base plugged in and then another round of charging with the base (not plugged in) gives you plenty of hours. From what I recall, my drive to Orlando, Florida from Chicago was about 24 hours with stops and earbuds were still running strong.

Cons: Not much other than an issue I'm having is with initial bluetooth connectivity but it could be user error. Sometimes the app picks up some other brand device on bluetooth (like a beat maker light or speaker) and I don't even think I have that in the house. Also, after dealing with customer service, if battery is low (not dead), the bluetooth may not work properly. So if it's disconnected and you try to reconnect when battery low, it could be tricky. So those 24+ hours functionality could be less if you have disconnected the bluetooth with a low battery. Can't think of why it needs much energy to connect to a bluetooth or even it's 100% that issue.
Not a big gripe though. I just keep earbuds in when I'm using it. And when it starts to get low while in my ear I just make sure to put in in base to charge. And to make sure tokeep it at a good charge capacity when not in use. Also, I think the battery drains when not
text_fidelity_b: Soundcore by Anker Life P3 Noise Cancelling Earbuds, Ultra Long 50H Playtime, Fast Charging, Big Bass, Multi-Mode Noise Cancelling, AI-Enhanced Calls, Wireless Charging, App Control, Bluetooth 5.2

text_fidelity_a:
Sangean DT-210 FM-Stereo/AM PLL Synthesized Tuning Pocket Radio I don't usually purchase products that require earbuds because I have considerable hearing loss. However, I took a chance on this little radio and I am VERY glad I did. I can hear this radio extremely well -- it has a tremendous amount of volume power considering its size (4" long, about the size of a cell phone). It has AM & FM bands, stereo/mono setting, can be used w/out the earbuds as a regular radio. It also allows memory pre-sets of your favorite stations. The radio attaches to your belt via a removable plastic clip.

If you use hearing aids,you will need to remove them to use the earbuds, of course. I suppose you could try a different headset device -- one that can be used WITH hearing aids. I have found that I can hear this radio very well with the use of the earbuds. Again, my hearing loss is severe-to-profound, but I can hear this baby!

I HIGHLY recommend this radio for use with or without any type of headest. It takes two AAA batteries, which seem to last in this device a very long time!

A top-notch product! GO FOR IT!
text_fidelity_b: Sangean DT-210 FM-Stereo/AM PLL Synthesized Tuning Pocket Radio

text_fidelity_a:
KZ ZS10 Pro, Linsoul 4BA+1DD 5 Driver in Ear Monitor, HiFi Metal Earphones, with Stainless Steel Faceplate, 2 Pin Detachable Cable (Without Mic, Black) Best sounding in-ear headphones I've ever heard, by a mile. I've owned the Bang and Olufsen H3, Sony XBA H1, Klipsch S4, X7, X6i, 1More Dual Drivers, Beats by Dr Dre Tour (wired), and Monster Cable's Jamz and Turbines.

The bass has lots of range and goes DEEP, in some tracks it even reminds me of my Kicker CVR 12' car subwoofer I used to blast about 15 years ago. It is not quite that overpowering, of course, and it balances out nicely with the other frequencies. The midrange is very present and natural sounding judging by how vocals and guitar strings sound. The highs are beautiful, they sound very accurate to me and present no sibilance. The overall sound is very rich and detailed, it allows you to follow specific instruments as you listen, and it even presents some soundstage (which I didn't think was possible in in-ears, maybe my aforementioned B&O H3 had some)

Overall these do have a V sound signature with boosted bass and treble, but not as marked as almost everything else that's in the market. In order to eliminate any fatigue caused by this, I would strongly recommend that you disable any bass boost, make sure you're not elevating bass or treble at all in EQ, and go even deeper and disable default features like Dolby Atmos (Oneplus phone) and even the Hi Fi quad DAC on LG phones (which I've found does introduce a bit of a V curve itself)

Other than their sound these earphones' build quality seems very good and durable. I'm in disbelief they could cost $60. You're welcome
text_fidelity_b: KZ ZS10 Pro, Linsoul 4BA+1DD 5 Driver in Ear Monitor, HiFi Metal Earphones, with Stainless Steel Faceplate, 2 Pin Detachable Cable (Without Mic, Black)

text_fidelity_a:
VIZIO SB3820-C6 38-Inch 2.0 Channel Sound Bar The sound from this bar is clean, clear, crisp and LOUD! A very decent amount of BASS, with a sub woofer output should you want to connect one. I found out I ordered a longer bar than is recommended. How did I find out? The packaging for this bar states that it is for a 42" or larger TV. I purchased it for a 32" TV. The concern, I believe, is that if the speakers are too far from the TV's center it will not seem as though the audio is coming from the actors. My brain is making the leap and tricking me so all is well. I use my TV for music for the most part anyway (Comcast Music Choice and Fire TV Music).
It is disappointing that Fire TV Music has such poor audio quality since it is there that I can make personal music choices unlike Comcast. Fire TV just sounds plain bad. It did on the TV speakers and now on the bar; it is just un-listenable. Safe to call it "LOW FIDELITY"
As far as connecting an input to this bar from your TV you have many options and most all the cables you may need are included. I really liked that they included the cord to to connect the bar to a sub. This cord is over and above what is required to connect the bar to the TV...very nice touch VIZIO. Now I need to go to my storage and try to find my sub :-)
My TV only offers 2 audio outputs, head phone and optical. Included with the bar were a headphone-to-2 RCA connector cord, and a fiber optic patch cord, among others. That allowed me what would be considered the worst quality connection and the best quality connection possibilities. If you don't have OPTICAL OUT on your TV do not despair...the worst possible option (headphone-to-RCA patch cord) sounds FANTASTIC! I can detect no loss of fidelity between the two. You will not be missing out.
Now to the reason I gave it 3 stars rather than 5. The back of the remote just keeps sliding off. It is not broken in any way. Just poorly designed. I often use the sound bar in dark or nearly dark conditions. It is taking time to train myself to not go where I normally would to use the any of the buttons. So how about the POWER button? It is not the top left button on the remote as you will see and are used to on any other remote in your home. For some strange reason instead of the power button being in the far upper left of the remote they felt this was a good place to position the INPUT button. Power is upper right. Volume UP/DOWN is traditionally placed on the left side of the remote with a paddle switch or separate buttons. Located in the standard volume UP/DOWN positions are the TruVolume and the TruSurround HD. The volume UP/DOWN are located on a FLAT 1-3/8" (34.9mm) x 1-3/8" (34.9mm) multi-function EVER SO SLIGHTLY RAISED square. To be honest I can't even tell that it IS raised at all most of the time. If you go for the volume in low light you may operate any of 3 other function controls. Lastly, if you were hoping the VOLUME controls are the 2 well raised buttons on the right (traditional location) you would be wrong. Those are your BASS/TREBLE controls.
I am not sure I would buy this bar again knowing what I do now about the remote. As I said I often use the remote in low or no light. The problems I mention here may just be my own...but I doubt it. All of these tiny buttons and controls are all scrunched into a small 2-3/8" (60.3mm) x 1-3/8" (34.9mm) upper 40% of this little remote and they are not raised enough and not far apart enough to be used just by touch. I well believe that just 3 functions on the remote will account for 90% of it's use. POWER (that CAN be felt but it is in the wrong place...you'll get used to that) and the VOLUME UP/DOWN that exist on a square, fully smooth (NO tactile feedback...I'd hate to see a blind person trying to operate), 4-function piece of plastic that is raised about 1/32" (0.8mm). On the bright side for me, I found out fairly quickly that my cable box remote controls the basic functions of the sound bar. I hope you get so lucky.
Knowing what I know now I should have purchased a bar in the 28"-32" (71mm-81mm) class looking for features such as the control panel on the bar being mildly illuminated and a proper remote perhaps with illumination itself. My roommate may buy mine from me for a location that is always well lit and has a 42" TV. I'll lose $20 on the deal but I can get the absolute right bar for me.. I don't return items that are not what I would like due to my own failure in researching. So, for better or worse, the bar is mine. There is one thing you cannot fault; THIS THING SOUNDS AMAZING!
- Good Shopping!!!
text_fidelity_b: VIZIO SB3820-C6 38-Inch 2.0 Channel Sound Bar

text_fidelity_a:
Wacom Intuos Intuos4 - Medium I will preface this review by stating that I am not a graphic artist and I have the artistic ability of a common garden rock. I did not get this tablet for doing artwork. As such, I have a different perspective on this product than the majority of people who buy an Intuos4.

I am very new to working with tablets and I started with a basic Bamboo small. This was a great little tablet, but the important word there was "little". I upgraded to an Intuos4 Medium because I wanted a bigger tablet, and I have been delighted with it. I do not use this tablet in the way a true artists would use it, but I have gained a deep appreciation for it nevertheless.

Because of the work I do, I use computers very frequently. I use them at home too, which is where I've attached my Intuos4. I am always looking for ways to make computing more comfortable, and on a whim I tried tablets. I discovered that, for me, tablet pens are more pleasant with which to work than mice.

The Intuos, in particular, is a good fit with an excellent digital pen that is designed well and fits my hand comfortably. The feel is right, and when writing the nib/tablet contact feels very much like writing on paper with a pencil. There are multiple nibs too, as well as additional pens for purchase, that make finding the right combination easy. So far, I have used only the default nib that was in the pen when I opened the box, and I am satisfied.

There is also a mouse in the package that works for most generic purposes but I rarely touch it. It is a no-frills, three-button scrolling mouse that is actually not bad, but it is only used on the writing surface of the tablet.

My primary use of this tablet is for writing, not drawing, and I have found the handwriting recognition software that is activated with the driver install to be mostly reasonable with translating my chicken scratches. It does have a bad tendency, however, to translate my lowercase letter "b" to "6" or sometimes even "d". As a result of this and other minor quirks I have changed my writing mannerisms to give the software better accuracy, and these new mannerisms are so habitual that I find that when I am writing on paper I have carried these new habits with me to that medium.

The tablet is much more pressure sensitive than my Bamboo was and when I make an effort to either bear down or lighten up with the pressure I can see the difference. This is especially true when using artistry software like Corel Painter. For serious artists, the Intuos4 offers 2048 pressure levels which should suffice for most.

I've made no use of the buttons on my Intuos4 but I use the Touch Ring frequently for scrolling. This is an excellent substitute for a scroll wheel, though it is not critical for my uses.

The pen and tablet are NOT useful for everything. For example, it's a bad choice for playing FPS games like Unreal Tournament. For chess, sudoku, working in MS Word or even grunching numbers in a spreadsheet, it is very workable.

Ok, so why do I prefer this higher-end tablet over a Bamboo Fun? I tried a Bamboo Fun Pen and Touch, which is a tablet that is more in line with people of my skill level (rank beginner and home user). That said, I could not get comfortable with the Pen and Touch, and I feel the Intuos4 pen is a much better for for my hands. Also, the Touch portion was awkward for me. The Intuos4 just works better for me, plain and simple.

For a non-artist, the Intuos4 Medium Tablet is a high-dollar item that can possibly be looked at as an unnecessary expense. For me, though, it is a blessing in that it makes most tasks on the computer more comfortable and easy. I am hooked on this tablet and recommend it to anyone who is either a serious artist looking for a good digital tablet or someone like me who just wants to be comfortable while working on the computer. It is a serious input device and will change the way you interact with the computer.
text_fidelity_b: Wacom Intuos Intuos4 - Medium

text_fidelity_a:
Kindle Paperwhite E-reader (Previous Generation - 7th) - Black, 6" High-Resolution Display (300 ppi) with Built-in Light, Wi-Fi + Free Cellular Connectivity - Includes Special Offers For years, I used the keyboard kindle after it first came out and loved the "classic" look of the page so much. After replacing it several times due to screen issues, I finally made the switch to the paperwhite with some skepticism, thinking the back-light would make it into yet another screen I look at. I was pleasantly surprised that even the brighter settings still look like a page, and I can turn it all the way down for the same effect as my older model kindle. Plus, I don't need to bother anyone with a light anymore when I read in bed, in the car at night, etc.

Paying a bit extra for no ads was worth it, and I enjoy the drawings that serve as screensavers. The home page is not my favorite - I would prefer to default to my library list instead of wading through recommendations, etc. - but it's not that much of a hassle to tap over to the library screen. When I'm reading a book, it automatically opens to the page I left off on just like my old kindle.

I only vaguely miss having the 3G function my old kindle had because I used to live out in the boonies with limited internet access. However, the WiFi has been generally sufficient and now I just make sure I download a few books before I travel.

Overall, the kindle has definitely revolutionized the way I read since it first came out when I was in high school. I do still keep a lot of hard copies of my favorite series and enjoy reading real books from time to time, but the kindle is SO easy to download anything, anytime you want. Not to mention bringing a whole library with you in one slim package while traveling! I have had this model for a year and a half now, and have no issues or complaints at this time.
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Paperwhite E-reader (Previous Generation - 7th) - Black, 6" High-Resolution Display (300 ppi) with Built-in Light, Wi-Fi + Free Cellular Connectivity - Includes Special Offers

I found that I had to fiddle with them constantly to hit the sweet spot for the music to sound like it should instead of like I was listening through a tin can, and while fiddling with them the touch controls become an annoying hassle because you are trying to get the fit right and the music is turning on and off and pausing and skipping, etc, because you are touching them. The buds can't seem to differentiate at all between an actual hold/grip to manipulate them in your ears, and a tap as you would do to actually use a touch control feature.

Don't quote me on this because it's not like I counted every review that appeared male vs female, but I found that they hurt and I think it might be because they were designed by somewhat larger-eared males. I originally assumed the hurty issue was likely because they were designed by some 60 year old man engineer with huge ears (because ears grow our whole lives) and so they were only made to fit kind of older larger ears. I even wrote on my Samsung review that they should have made the fit for the age group of their customer. But now, reading these Amazon reviews, I am noticing that the people saying they fit great seem to mostly be male names and those saying they hurt seem to mostly be female-normative names, so I still think they were designed for larger ears, but maybe for males they will fit better - I truly don't know how different in size male vs female ears are though; it's just a random observation of these reviews of hurt vs feel great.

Bottom line, they hurt my ears and were too picky about being perfectly aligned in my ear. On the rare occasion I hit that sweet spot they sounded great and never felt like they were going to fall out. Too bad it took so much effort to find that spot.
text_fidelity_b: SAMSUNG Galaxy Buds Live True Wireless Bluetooth Earbuds w/ Active Noise Cancelling, Charging Case, AKG Tuned 12mm Speaker, Long Battery Life, US Version, Mystic Red

Surge Protector Power Strip - Flat Plug Extension Cord, TROND 8 Widely-Spaced Outlets, 4 USB Charger(1 USB C Port), 5FT Ultra Thin Cord, 1440J, Flat Wall Plug, Desk Charging Station for Travel, White The TROND Flat Plug Power Strip Surge Protector is a great concept. Everything about it shows that some thought has been given to its design. Unfortunately, their choice of materials weren't as well thought out.

Some design concepts that attracted me to this surge protector is that it gives you 8 power plugs in a surface area that's just under 4 x 4 inches. The four plugs at the top are grounded while the 4 on the side are two-prongs. In addition, the wall plug is flat, giving you a lot of options as to where you can plug this product in. Finally, there are three USB-A ports and one USB-C port.

However, as I've mentioned, some design choices are questionable. As with many surge protectors, the USB ports are under-powered. The Type-A ports are not too bad at 5V/2.4A, but there is no quick charge capability. The Type-C is not PD, so your charging options are no better than the Type-A ports. You're stuck with 5V/3A with a total wattage shared between them at 14W or 3.4A.

My second gripe is with the build material. Compared to many power strips, the plastic covering this product feels quite cheap. It has a smooth texture and just feels... thin to the touch. The same plastic also covers the wall plug. In addition, the power wire is thinner than other power strips that you'll find. They feel more like the two-prong extension cords, except that it has three wires.

Now, I don't have proof that their choice of materials will be an issue at all, but it does give me pause.
text_fidelity_b: Surge Protector Power Strip - Flat Plug Extension Cord, TROND 8 Widely-Spaced Outlets, 4 USB Charger(1 USB C Port), 5FT Ultra Thin Cord, 1440J, Flat Wall Plug, Desk Charging Station for Travel, White

text_fidelity_a:
JOBY UltraFit Sling Strap for Women Horribly Uncomfortable.

What's the one thing that makes a good neck strap comfortable for long term wearing? Padding. What's the one thing this strap is completely lacking? Padding!

The part of the strap that's supposed to go around your neck is a two inch wide very rough textured bit of nylon webbing. Seat belts are softer than this material. The first time I tried the Joby UltraFit Sling Strap I carried my Kodak Z990 around for about an hour and it was so uncomfortable. Who designs a neck strap with NO padding?

This strap attaches to your camera via the ¼" tripod screw mount on the bottom of the camera. It's odd that your camera hangs upside down and I don't like the single point of failure mounting. Also, because of the way it's designed it puts angular force on the mounting threads when hanging and even more when releasing or engaging the quick release latch. Since the threads in my Kodak are plastic I have even more dislike for this mounting system. Additionally, you have to dismount your strap any time you want to use a tripod or monopod.

I found in the time I used this that the only time the (non) padded portion of the strap is on your neck is when the rig is retracted when you use the 'Speed Cinch' to bring the camera up for shooting, at least on my extra large frame, the whole strap rotates forward and puts the even more uncomfortable thinner strap around your neck and the 'padded' section down on your chest.

To sum it up... it's uncomfortable. It completely lacks any padding. It has an odd mounting system that puts lever like force on your tripod socket and you have to take the strap off to use a tripod or monopod. text_fidelity_a:
Samsung Galaxy Tab 2 (10.1-Inch, Wi-Fi) 2012 Model I thought long and hard about a tablet, knowing that for me it would basically be a toy. Plus I already had a Nook Color. When the iPad2 reduced in price, I thought about getting one of those, but decided against it for the following reasons: (1) no Flash--and yes, I know HTML5 is going to make that obsolete, but in the meantime many websites have a lot of money invested in Flash animation and even restaurants use the silly format to show you their menus (geez, just give us a LIST already--I don't need pretty pictures to find out if you serve something I can eat) and (2) I'm already invested in the Android market and would have to buy many iPad apps that I already have free from Android.

I have not even used it for a week yet, but this a preliminary review with some information I saw requested in other reviews (not necessarily here at Amazon).

UPS delivered this a little before 6:30 p.m. I immediately plugged it into the charger and left it alone. It was charged by 10 p.m. (it might have been earlier, but the unit was away from me and I heard no bleep or flash that might have have indicated the charge was finished). So it does not take six or eight or ten hours to charge as I have seen claimed on other sites. By midnight I was attached to wireless, had gotten into all my accounts and Android apps and was happily surfing and rearranging my home screen.

I used this over the weekend at a science fiction convention. I did not use it constantly, but turned the screen on and off all day for about a 12-hour period, reading Facebook and blogs, checking the news and weather, looking at the convention schedule online, playing short You Tube videos, etc. Nothing excessive, but sometimes did have it on for a half hour to 45-minutes at the time. I also do not have a lot of widgets going, like the Accu-Weather and news widgets that come pre-loaded on the home screen. (They delete easily.) In that 12-hour period it never got below 78% on the battery. It's very quick and fast and responds to a Targus stylus (rubber tipped) wonderfully, much better than my Nook color. The resolution of the screen is impressive. Maybe it's not the new iPad's "retinal display," but it's very, very sharp and bright, even though I keep my brightness turned down to save power. I downloaded the Nook app and the magazines I subscribe to look gorgeous and are simple to read; if not, a tap of the screen makes the text bigger. The unit also comes with Zinio preloaded, an app I plan to use to subscribe to non-US magazines. Kindle books look nice as well, but to me this is too large for marathon reading sessions. I prefer my Nook Color for that. Like my Android phone and my Nook Color, it connects to wireless like a dream, which is more than I can say for my laptop.

Things that might lead you to choose another tablet: (1) The camera is nothing special. It takes good close ups, but further away was problematic. However, I was in a low-light situation each time. Taking photos outside may be totally different. Why Samsung chose to remove the flash I have no idea. Silly, really. But who buys a tablet to take pictures with? (2) With a stylus I can tap to enlarge an image (like Google Maps), but not make it smaller and there is no plus or minus sign on the screen as on my Android phone. (3) Blogger doesn't work in the browser; you have to download the Blogger app, but that works well. iExit doesn't work on it, either. Rats. (4) As at least one other person mentioned, the screen cap button is right in a place where you can hit it easily. I thought of a good use for it this weekend (took a screen cap of the online schedule for the convention I was at, made a short-cut of it to the screen, then pulled up the screen cap for reference rather than going to the web page all the time). Very convenient! (5) Hate the pre-loaded websites in the browser, but I have seen this on other tablets. Apparently we the public are stupid (or lazy) and can't find our own favorite websites and bookmark them. [eyes roll], and (6) my Bluetooth keyboard won't work with it right now because there is as yet no driver for Android 4.0 (Ice Cream Sandwich).

I hope to check back with further comments.

[A few weeks later after I bought this, my husband found an Asus Transformer (TF300) at a good price. It appears to be just as good as this Samsung and the camera is better. It has a zoom and does take a better photo. So if you were looking for a tablet with a better camera the Asus Transformer may be for you. Note: It doesn't have a flash either.]

[Update July 31, 2012 to answer "How long does the battery last"?: I was sick and tired of not seeing any Olympic equestrian coverage except for a couple of hours in the wee hours of the morning, so downloaded the "Live Extra" Olympics app from the Android Market. This carries live streaming of events as well as archived events. This morning I watched about two hours of live streaming of the jumping finals. When that ended I watched six hours of cross-country eventing replay. Then about an hour and forty minutes of the replay of the jumping. I had my brightness at about 35%. This got me down to 10% of the battery from a full charge. Quite satisfactory.]
text_fidelity_b: Samsung Galaxy Tab 2 (10.1-Inch, Wi-Fi) 2012 Model

text_fidelity_a:
Steiner Marine Binoculars for Adults and Kids, 7x50 Binoculars for Bird Watching, Hunting, Outdoor Sports, Wildlife Sightseeing and Concerts - Quality Performance Water-Going Optics , Black I bought these at the same time as a Steiner 7x50 Commander XP model. The Commander XP's use the same case but for triple the price have better eyepieces, coatings and optical specifications and a few additional or better accessories than the Marine model.

I compared them in terrestrial and celestial viewing but the easiest comparison is done with astronomical subjects since they really define performance clearly. The images in the Marine model merged effortless. In the Commander XP, I have difficulty merging the images. The XP's are obviously badly out of collimation. I don't care to fix this myself on binos in this price range but I was pleased that the much less costly Marine's appear to be flawless in this respect.

I evaluated the real and apparent fields of view as well as the sharpness near the edge of the field.

In the Marine model, the real field of view is reasonably wide but apparent field is quite narrow. It's not bad but it's not a spectacular vista either. In the Commander XP, the real FOV is only barely perceptibly wider. Steiner's website lists the specifications. The apparent field, which is not specified is about the same for both. The almost indiscernable extra width of real FOV does not contribute much to the value of the XP's for triple the price.

On the Marine model, I put Sirius and Jupiter in the center of the field. They each looked nice. Moving the binoculars so that the objects were farther from the center of the field I could see the image degraded about half-way to the edge of the field of view. Near the very edge, the image was appalling. Much more than half-way out of the center of the field of view, the star or planet turns from a bright point to just a smear. Near the very edge it's a dim smudge. I tried the same with the Commander XP. It was every bit as bad. I could have probably improved things a little by refocusing but that only means that the field isn't flat either.

Are the XP's better on dim objects? The optics are supposed to transmit 96% light compared to the Commander V's 95% and the Marine's 90%. I saw very little difference on dim objects like the Orion nebula or the background of the Pleides or Jupiter's moons. Again, I can't see the justification for triple the price, so I commend these Marine models over their far more costly cousins.

Both have generious eye-relief, 20mm for the Marine and 22mm for these XP's. They also have the same weight and dimensions. They're heavy but still reasonable if you're wearing a thick coat to pad your chest and a harness to keep them from swinging all over if you're moving. Also, at 7x they're reasonable for handholding. For me, 7x50 is about the limit for handholding. Heavier or higher power would be too shakey. 6x56 might be nicer if they were more common.

Where the XP is clearly better is with small details like the click-loc strap attachments (for use with Steiner straps and harnesses only), the better eyepiece covers, lens covers, focuser grips, shading eye-cups, and various doo-dads that come in the case. It comes with a flotation strap which the Marine doesn't, but I would still rather prefer a harness which neither comes with.

I bought these Porro prism binos because I thought for the high price, particularly the XP's, they should be outstanding. While roof prism binos might require fifteen hundred dollars or more to achieve optical exellence (or so I've heard), it should be easier with porros. With these, the optical quality is lacking nontheless. To be honest, I have nothing to compare them to. I've never seen better, but I was still totally underwhelmed by the performance which was only slightly better than I would expect from binoculars in the hundred dollar range. In the case of the XP's, it's a rip-off, no question. In the case of the Marine model, the value is closer to reasonable because of the far lower price. I didn't compare them to other binos in their price range. The Fujinon line would be the most similar but it would also be worthwhile to compare Nikons, even the well-regarded Monarch roof prism models which are in this price category but are totally different.

text_fidelity_a:
ACDelco 2-Hour Fast Battery Charger Includes AA Rechargeable Batteries and Car Adapter, 4 Count This charger works. It comes down to preference in style, and perhaps the going price at the time you are shopping around.

Upon arrival, I immediately unpacked this ACDelco battery charger. It comes with 4 AA batteries, and since I didn't see anything on the package about them being precharged, I went ahead and plugged them into my truck adapter. I was curious how well it would do in my truck (with the included car adapter) and since I knew I was running an errand that would take no more than two hours, I figured it was a good time to try it out.

I plugged them in at 2:10 pm, and saw that the batteries were charging as indicated by the red light. When I got back into my truck (I remembered to look!), the time was 3:05, and the battery indicator light was green, telling me that the batteries were fully charged. So this 55 minute charge time (likely less, since I wasn't in the truck whole time) tells me that it charged faster than anticipated, or the batteries had a little bit of charge on them to begin with, which is more apt the case--which is nice when they can be used right out of the package. Either way, it clearly charges and works fine.

(edit to add..) I see in the lower product description that the batteries come charged. Mine weren't fully charged, but I assume half charge (or more), and my charge time just topped them off. So to test this product further, I grabbed a set of drained rechargeable batteries from another brand that I hadn't gotten around to re-charging yet. I mean, I used them but drained them. I hadn't charged them again yet because I don't care for the charger it came with, so I just keep putting it off. I LIKE THIS CHARGING UNIT, and I will explain after details..

DETAILS!
--This charger charges AA and AAA batteries. It comes with 4 AA batteries and two styles of cords 110-volt wall adapter and 12-volt car adapter

-- The cord measurement for each is as follows:
74" wall charger cord
41" car adapter cord

--Charging Time Per Battery Capacity:
AA 1400mAh - 1800mAh: 1.5 - 2 hours
AA 1800mAh - 2300mAh: 2-2.5 hours
AAA 600mAh - 750mAh: 1.5 - 2 hours
AAA 750mAh - 1000mAh: 2-2.5 hours

--So, on the face of the charger on the left hand side, there are two indicator lights: one that glows red as the batteries charge, and one that glows green when charged and ready for use. Easy peasy.

--On the right hand side, there is a switch. It is to be set to either 2 batteries, or 4 batteries (+2, +4). Among the rebels among us, I have no idea what happens if we tried charging three batteries! :O

--Within the battery placement area, the slots are numbered. 1 through 4. I wish there were more clarification on this on the product page because I can no longer find the directions it came with. I am thinking that if just two batteries are being used, and they were placed in #1, #2 slots (or #3,#4) AND the indicator switched was in place for 2 batteries, does the charging juice primarily go to those spot (so as to keep with the quick charge ability)?. I think if just two batteries are being charged, then they go in the center, in the #1 and #2 spots-- so that's my plan going forward. I imagine this information is in the little pamphlet that came with the package. I'll be back if I find it and learn anything.

--The charging batteries at no point has gotten too warm my Energizer one gets pretty warm).

MY THOUGHTS:
--I LOVE that it has the TWO charging cords, with LONG cords. First, I like that it even has a cord, period. I have the Energiizer one that is just plugged into the wall. It seems like it would take up less space, but it doesn't. I find it harder to use as I need perfect clearance to plug that thing in. With this, I just need to find an outlet, then I can have it placed further away, making it easier to see and access. With the addition of the car charger, it just adds another option. Nice for camping (flashlights, radio, etc), or if you still use non cellphone cameras that eat batteries like crazy (this is what originally got me into rechargeable batteries almost 20 years ago, the digital cameras- ugh, I'm old). I sometimes bring a speaker with me for use with smartphone. It takes AA batteries. If I think to actually carry this unit around with me, I can charge my speaker batteries on the go if need be. But I think I will use this primarily in my home. I go through batteries with use of a couple of lighted mirrors. I have one that takes 4AAA and one that takes 4AA. The lights are bright, and I tend to go through batteries- so I make sure to have rechargeables on hand. As mentioned before, I like this unit because it is easier for me to find a place to put it to plug in AND have resting nearby. I had been in need of recharging a set of batteries and just hadn't gotten around to it because I don't care for the inconvenient (to me) charging unit of the other one. It works great, but I just found I prefer to have a cord. This has a cord.

PICTURES include another brand of (depleted) rechargeable AA battery (2000mah) with start time of being placed in charging unit. Product info says AA batteries between 1800mah and 2300mah will take 2-2.5 hours to charge. I put in the batteries at 11:42 am, and at 2:18 pm they were still charging. This would be just over 2.5 hours. I got up to take my dogs outside, and when I came back an hour later, the batteries were fully charged. So, I would plan on anywhere between 2.5-3.5 for a full charge on a depleted set of batteries (from another brand). Since I have yet to fully deplete the ACDelco batteries, I can't test those out until I do.

In summation.. I find nothing wrong with it, it works mostly intended.. If I figure anything else out as I continue to use these, I will be back to update.
text_fidelity_b: ACDelco 2-Hour Fast Battery Charger Includes AA Rechargeable Batteries and Car Adapter, 4 Count

Sony WHXB900N Noise Cancelling Headphones, Wireless Bluetooth Over the Ear Headset - Blue (Amazon Exclusive) Sony WH-XB900N Wireless Noise Canceling Extra Bass Headphones have great sound quality. Plus, for an over the ear headphone they are surprisingly lightweight. I also like how they bend to fold up and are really pliable. However, that's really where the greatness stops. Pairing these with any device I own is difficult or doesn't happen at all. These will not pair with my laptop. My laptop sees it's there. It claims it's playing from the headphones, but alas it does not most of the time. In addition, these will not play from iTunes. So, if you have an Apple device forget it. These will not pair with my iPhone 5. For two reasons, first, these are terrible with Apple devices/software and second, you must have the App to pair the headphones, which if you have an older phone won't happen because the App is only compatible with certain iOS systems. As much as I am angry with Apple for stopping all updates for older Apple devices (which work just fine otherwise), it's equally frustrating with App developers who do not design their Apps to be compatible with the older systems. So, most of my experience with these headphones is through the AUX jack.

Therefore, the sound quality is really good. I listen to a lot of hiphop and the bass is spot on. However, I do listen other types of music (pretty much everything) and I would have to say listening to Beethoven's 6th and Old Blind Dogs was a nice experience as well! The noise cancelling is a joke. I can hear everything around me still. In fact, I'm currently wearing these as I type this review and can hear the click clack of the keys, my son bump around upstairs, and my father just call my name. So, if you wear these on public transportation or at work, you're gonna hear everything as usual. But they are good headphones and comfortable on my ears.

The instructions are ridiculous. Can we stop with the picture instructions? They make no sense. I need words and should not have to depend on internet video reviews to get clarity on how to use anything. There is a way to play, pause, volume down/up by tapping or swiping, but I have no idea how to do it. Sometimes it works, sometimes not. They have a long battery life. I charged these weeks ago and they still have a charge as I use them now.

So, these have a great sound quality, the noise cancellation doesn't do anything, and you need to pair these with non-Apple devices.

text_fidelity_a:
VIOFO Dash Cam Front and Rear 2K 1440P 60fps +1080P 30fps Dual Dash Camera with Wi-Fi GPS, Emergency Recording, Motion Detection, 24h Parking Mode, Super Capacitor (A129 Plus Duo) This is a terrific kit, complete with everything to get you started... Some important notes...

1.) If you already have a camera in place that uses mini usb, then half the battle is already won. Most of these cameras use mini usbs.

2.) The Viofo has a capacitor battery, which is what you want, especially if you live in the hot areas. They are not prone to ballooning like lithium batteries.

3.) Instructions say to slide the camera onto a mounting plate, which has an adhesive backing, you then remove the adhesive cover and stick entire unit on the glass. But it comes to you preinstalled, at least mind was. All you have to do is peel the adhesive cover and stick the unit onto your glass. Out of curiosity, I tried to remove the plate, but I couldn't, it is very tight. So if you stick the unit to your window, taking it down for whatever reason will be a pain. I don't see how you can dismount the camera and leave the plate on the window. You would have to take the plate with you, which means ripping the adhesive from the glass.

So here's my tip... I'd like to be able to remove the camera, fiddle with it, change settings, etc. without hassle. Or perhaps, even dismount and hide my camera in the glove compartment when I need to. If you install it the way they tell you to, you will never take this camera down. My solution for this is using strong round earth magnets. I installed a round earth magnet on the back of the unit. This is easy, since it already has an adhesive back, just remove the cover and stick a magnet on it. Then I install another one directly onto the glass. These neodymium magnets are very strong and the hold is absolutely solid. This is how I install dashcams for myself and family. I have not installed the rearview, but I'll be using the same method. This is another review using the same method: https://www.amazon.com/gp/customer-reviews/RETFFEWXHSOJ6/ref=cm_cr_getr_d_rvw_ttl?ie=UTF8&ASIN=B088B6372Z

This is a 5-Star kit!
text_fidelity_b: VIOFO Dash Cam Front and Rear 2K 1440P 60fps +1080P 30fps Dual Dash Camera with Wi-Fi GPS, Emergency Recording, Motion Detection, 24h Parking Mode, Super Capacitor (A129 Plus Duo)

text_fidelity_a:
D-Link Wi-Fi Camera with Remote Viewing (DCS-930L) (Discontinued by Manufacturer) Compared to a similar camera made by Belkin, setting up the D-Link was kind of a pain. Not as much of a pain as setting up a Foscam F18918W - where you get directed to a third party domain name provider and get to learn the joys of port forwarding - but a relative hassle.

For the Belkin, I opened the box, plugged into my router, ran a set up program that took less than five minutes, downloaded an app, and I was up and running. While this is a very similar product in both look and function, it took over an hour - and two ethernet cables - to set it up. There is no Mac software on the installation cd. The box states that a Windows pc is required, but the website has a Mac download available. You have to scroll through the product photos, which aren't in alphanumeric order. Just keep looking until you find the DCS-930L - AFTER the 931L and the 932L and the 934L. Have faith. Keep going. It's there.

Once you get the program installed, it takes very little time to *find* the camera and teach it to log into your wireless network. And then you are back to the website to set up your account and view your camera. Except you are on a Mac, and the viewer requires you to install the Java Runtime Environment. JRE is a big old security vulnerability on Macs. So much so that Apple advises against using it. Mavericks lets you turn it on case by case - and, by default, it will ask you every time before running it. If you are on an OS below Mavericks, check the googles for setting your preferences so that you're not running JRE all the time.

Okay, so now you've got JRE going, and the first thing the program tells you is that you have to update your firmware AND you need to have the camera AND your computer ethernet-jacked right into your router. LOLWUT? I'm lucky. I am on a laptop, and I have an extra ethernet cable and an empty port. So, I did that, and there I was, up and running, about an hour, hour and a half, thereabouts, after I started.

Image quality is pretty good - not great. Audio is okay. The settings are very customizable. But the wifi receiver is very weak, and that limits the usefulness of this product.
text_fidelity_b: D-Link Wi-Fi Camera with Remote Viewing (DCS-930L) (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

text_fidelity_a: Amazon Basics SDHC Class 4 16GB Secure Digital Card the plus to this card is obvious--it has a large capacity.  The con is that it is a little slow in picture-taking.  Depending on what you're looking for, you may be happy or dissatisfied. I used it in a Kodak flip-style camcorder/still picture taker and I liked the fact that I didn't have to worry about filling up the card.  I recorded at 720 and it did fine in the recording and in the downloading of the video--I really didn't notice any speed issues.  Picture-taking was a different story; there was a noticeable lag in taking still photos. I wouldn't dismiss this card for that reason, however, unless a difference of a second or so will matter to you.  Most of my still picture taking on vacation is done with a larger point and shoot Canon IS, so the lag time with the little camera didn't matter much to me as I either used it mostly for video as mentioned or took stills of landscape or posed photos.  To be honest, I prefer not to use such a large capacity card for photos anyway as I have a fear of something going wrong with the card and losing hundreds of photos as opposed to a few videos.  So I'm happy to keep this in the little compact video camera and snap the occasional slow photo. I wouldn't put it in my Canon for the above reason and also because the photos I take with that I'd be more concerned about the sluggish picture-taking.  Be selective about how you use it, and I think you'll be more than satisfied
text_fidelity_b: Amazon Basics SDHC Class 4 16GB Secure Digital Card

text_fidelity_a: Polaroid Originals OneStep 2 VF - Summer Blue (9016) My youngest son graduated from high school this past weekend. I wanted him to be able to capture memories. Kids today use their cameras, but never go on to print out the photos. Of course, I am from a generation where we use to print out photos and scrapbook or place them in a photobook. Instead kids today Instagram or Snapchat, simply posting a memory that will be gone if those platforms crash. So, I instead am trying to get my son to capture some moments on film. The Polaroid Original One Step 2 provided gives him that option. Simply point and shoot. Instant fun, instant prints, instant memories captured.  I remember begging for a Polaroid when I was younger.  My parents said that they were expensive, and it seemed to take some time before “Santa” gave me one. But once I did, I enjoyed snapping photos and waiting those few minutes until the photo came to life before my eyes. So really, this is more nostalgic than practical. I wanted my son to know the wonder of a Polaroid. So of course, this review is from that prospective. The One Step 2 is easy to load. There is a built-in flash and other great features. Unlike the old Polaroids, this one has a built-in rechargeable battery. That’s a very nice feature. The only thing is that this camera DOES NOT come with film, but that was pretty easy to rectify. I simply ordered mine on Amazon. While some would say that the film is kind of expensive, 8 pics for about $18.00 which equals a little over $2 a photo, it is FUN and the exciting thing is now you can get black & white film. How much fun is that? Start capturing your memories. 4 stars.
text_fidelity_b: Polaroid Originals OneStep 2 VF - Summer Blue (9016)

SquareTrade 4-year Office Protection Plan Purchased this 4 year plan in November 2016 on a Dell Laser Printer. Thus the printer was a little over 2 years when it started doing weird things and I made a claim.

Basically ... the printer stopped printing black ... it just got lighter and lighter. I attempted to clean the heads and change the cartridges to no avail. The printer would also keep running and not stop after done doing a printer job.

I printed my receipt / invoice off Amazon to PDF. I then went to SquareTrade's website attached the receipt. I then made a claim. The claim process was pretty easy and they actually approved me for a full refund. I just needed to fill out an affidavit. I did this but a week later I still had no refund. Somehow my affidavit didn't get logged even though I got a confirmation email. I called them on the telephone and they fixed everything and were kind about it. Within 24 hours they emailed me an Amazon gift certificate (my choice) which gave me an additional 5% back. I this received a $121 refund on an $118 printer that died in its 3rd year.

I have no complaints and would purchase a square trade warranty again.

Bits of interest as I read other people's low reviews:

1) You purchase a 4 year warranty, but really, for example, it is just 3 extra years beyond the purchase's original 1 year warranty (or however long applies). If your item dies in a year, you have to go to the manufacturer for help.

2) You need to have your receipt. No biggie. Amazon is super amazing that way. I can see all my order back to when Amazon just sold books. Print the invoice / receipt to PDF and there you go. Receipt. Proof of purchase.

3) There is no paper copy of this plan. This is great. It saves trees. You would probably lose it anyway. But Amazon also kept a copy of the fact that I purchased this along with the printer. It was in my order history. There is your proof and all the telephone numbers are there. It is so easy. You don't need a stack of papers.

4) If you file a claim and get 100% of your purchase price back, you cannot file a claim for the same item again. No brainer.

5) This isn't accident insurance. If you do a dumb thing like leave your camera on top of your husband's big rig fender and it ends up in a million pieces 1/2 mile from your house ... it is NOT covered. If you think it should be ... well then ... Take out an insurance policy ... not a warranty. Those are two different things.

6) If you got a deal and paid $65 for your item, but the item now sells for $400 ... you still only paid $65 and $65 is all you are getting back. You don't make money off warranties.
text_fidelity_b: SquareTrade 4-year Office Protection Plan

ELECOM Relacon Handheld Trackball Mouse, Thumb Control, 2.4GHz Wireless, Ergonomic Design, 10-Button Function with Smooth Tracking, Windows11, MacOS (M-RT1DRBK) I've bought and currently use both variants of the Relacon mouse. I'm putting this review on the wireless version.

Overall, 5 stars for the wireless with dongle, 3 stars for the Bluetooth. Unfortunately the Bluetooth one is a bit choppy with tracking, causing the pointer to jump to a random place on the screen often enough to be annoying. The dongle one doesn't have this issue for me. Otherwise they're identical in function and feel.

As a dedicated thumb trackball user since the early 90s, I love it! It is much better quality than any other ambidextrous thumb trackball I've optimistically tried over the years when looking for an alternative to the standard right (or rare left) dedicated handed thumb trackball. I have never been able to get comfortable or quick with finger trackballs, no matter how much I have wanted to or worked at it. Same with the Thinkpad trackpoint.

It is a physical relief to have a mouse that I can use in a neutral wrist position without having my hand or arm stretched out. It is especially nice to be able to transfer and use the mouse with my left hand when I need to type or do something else with my right.

I haven't installed the software or tried to remap the buttons. I just plug in the dongle or pair with Bluetooth, and Windows recognizes it. Since my displays are 1080 or smaller, I keep the speed or acceleration or dpi setting at 1 blink. The button is below the power switch, so I do accidentally tap it occasionally, but it's quick and easy to cycle back to 1.

The stand is more stylish than functional, and even with practice the mouse will sometimes slide right off, but at least it's included. Most of the time, I just switch it off and set the mouse on its side.
text_fidelity_b: ELECOM Relacon Handheld Trackball Mouse, Thumb Control, 2.4GHz Wireless, Ergonomic Design, 10-Button Function with Smooth Tracking, Windows11, MacOS (M-RT1DRBK)

I have an extensive technology background so I did not bother to read the manual beforehand and had no problems following what were simple on-screen instructions. And to Roku's credit, there were few of those. To be clear - you absolutely need a wireless internet router (WiFi) and a computing device to perform a few simple steps in order to install and activate the Roku HD. Including date entry and the time to explain some things to my friend for whom I was setting this up, the total time to get it running was less than 15 minutes.

- Establishing your account. You will need some form of computing platform to access the Roku site via the web and complete this step. It's relatively painless.

- Payment options: you can use a credit card or a Paypal account. I believe the latter is a relatively new option that shows that Roku is paying attention to complaints registered in these reviews. The Payment option is there to remove barriers to adding for pay services. Of course, it makes it so easy that you are almost lured into it. Smart move on their part. Just be careful because fees can add up.

- Remote Control - Information that needed to be entered with the remote is a bit awkward at first, but I quickly adapted to it. One note about the remote: it is what we engineering geeks call elegant. Simple, functional with only the essential buttons. I absolutely loved the Netflix, Pandora and Crackle bottoms to quickly get most users to popular services. I would have loved it if Hulu Plus had a button since that is the service my friend plans to use. But that would have detracted from the elegance factor.

- Manual: Although I did not need the manual to set ths device up, I did take the time to read through it afterwards to make sure my non-technical friend could depend on it if a problem arose. I was impressed with the clarity and how well the technical writing team made it simple, friendly and anticipated possible support problems by weaving in information that would preclude those.

The default channels were merely OK, but a good start. The free content, especially from Crackle It, did not excite me nor my friend who would be using it.

A word about economics: the friend for whom I purchased this and set it up wanted this so she could scale back on expenses. At one point she was paying approximately seventy dollars a month for cable service. She scaled that back to local channels that entailed a monthly recurring charge of three times the monthly fee of Hulu Plus. In fact, had she wanted, she could get Hulu Plus and Netflix's unlimited content for two thirds of what she is paying monthly for local cable channels, and nearly a fifth of the cost of her original subscription that did not provide near the content of Hulu Plue and Netflix combined.

It's easy to see that this device pays for itself in very short order if you deem that the content from the services that you can stream via the Roku is as good for your purposes as the content you are currently getting from cable or satellite services. Everyone will have a different breakeven point after which your return on the initial investment is substantial. If you are considering this device do a little analysis. Of course, make sure the services to which you will subscribe with the Roku meet your needs.

There are also services at various price levels that allow you to stream video, music and send photos directly from your PC or Mac to your TV via the service, which sends that content to your Roku. Four such services that you can easily find via a search of the web are: Roksbox, Play on, Chaneru and RoConnect.

This device is so cool that I was tempted to get one for myself. I have not subscribed to any cable or satellite services for nearly a decade, but I do purchase a lot of DVDs and spend far too much time on YouTube. I am still on the fence, but was disappointed in the lack of YouTube support, and was not impressed with the available workarounds and services. The most promising, RateRix, seemed to me to be kludgy and unreliable. I was also put off by Netflix, which wanted me to sign up before I could ascertain that they had the content I was looking for. One part of their FAQ mentioned that their mail service was still available and had vastly more videos than their streaming service. Since I watch a lot of foreign langiage films, as well as jazz performances and concerts I decided that the Roku would not meet my immediate needs. One other (and puzzling) deal breaker for me is the Roku will not stream my music stored on Amazon's cloud. That is odd considering that it will stream music from Pandora and video from Amazon, but not music from Amazon.

UPDATE (JULY 8, 2012): While my friend continues to love her Roku, I found an alternate streaming solution that gives me access to YouTube and even more content: [[ASIN:B00882OHL0 D-Link MovieNite Plus Streaming Media Player]]. See my July 8, 2012 review that compares and contrasts that device with the Roku,

I am an old curmudgeon who is set in my ways. This device certainly met the entertainment and economic needs of my friend, and I am sure that anyone who pays for TV services has the potential to greatly benefit from it. The device is beautifully designed, not only from an engineering perspective, but also from a human-factors perspective. The minute Roku works a deal with Google for a YouTube channel is the minute I purchase one. I have a feeling that will happen sooner than later. In the meantime, the smile on my friend's face when this was up and running is proof of its value.
text_fidelity_b: Roku HD Streaming Player (Old Model)

text_fidelity_a:
Crucial X6 4TB Portable SSD - Up to 800MB/s - PC and Mac - USB 3.2 USB-C External Solid State Drive - CT4000X6SSD9 Crucial is one of the first names that comes to mind when I have needed reliable RAM for my systems in the past. I have a Crucial 500MB SSD in one of my systems and it has served me well over the years so I was interested in this SSD as a back-up option for pictures and data. It has proven to be a fine solution for my needs.

Right up front – yes, it works with Linux right out of the box. I plugged it into my Peppermint Linux system and the kernel immediately recognized the drive and made it available. It was on me to mount the drive, but this was a simple matter and I was able to access the file system and see drive statistics. Obviously it works with Windows so I won’t go into that.

This is a physically small device, slightly less than half the size of a cell phone (iPhone 6s is what I used for comparison). It will easily fit inside the change pocket in my jeans and can tuck just about anywhere. This is a double-edged sword. On one hand it is convenient to have something this small and easy to store, but it is also easy to misplace or even lose. If this stays in your laptop bag or briefcase it should be secure, but if you are in a habit of keeping things in your pockets instead be cautious.

Transfer speeds are good. I have not done benchmarks on this drive but I copied thousands of pictures (average size about 8mb per file, some more and some less) and it was significantly faster than the USB drive I have been using for a while and faster than many of the thumb drives I have been using for backups. I have no complaints.

This is a small and fast drive that just works. It works with Linux which for me is important, and it is small enough to tuck in my camera bag for making backups in the field.
text_fidelity_b: Crucial X6 4TB Portable SSD - Up to 800MB/s - PC and Mac - USB 3.2 USB-C External Solid State Drive - CT4000X6SSD9

As soon as I selected the Roku HDMI input the on-screen image dramatically improved. Checking the same Netflix movies and shows as before, it was always much brighter and more vibrant than when using built-in streaming. Images on other services like Hulu were also quite watchable.
I was going to return the set until I hooked up the Roku. With the improved image coming from the HDMI input, my wife and I will give it a week's trial.
I would strongly not recommend this set if you intend to use its internal ("smart") capability. text_fidelity_a:
SAMSUNG (MB-ME32GA/AM) 32GB 95MB/s (U1) microSDHC EVO Select Memory Card with Full-Size Adapter So far so good on this micro sD card.

This is the third micro sD card I’ve bought for my phones since October 2015.

The other two were the 32GB EVO Class 10 Micro SDHC up to 48MB/s with Adapter (MB-MP32DA/AM). And, I was definitely elated to see those were no longer available. Sorry that it is mean-spirited, but after knowing why – I think anyone would be happy to see a fault product go away.

Why did I choose this one?

I purchased the 32GB EVO Class 10 Micro SDHC up to 48MB/s with Adapter (MB-MP32DA/AM) in October of 2015 for my Samsung GS4, and only two (2) months later – I needed a brand new one. Why? It failed. No warning, nothing. Just a failure. The phone wasn’t dropped, shocked, or smashed. It had NO water damage either.

And this wouldn’t be the first failure either for that particular model.

The sD card I bought in December failed as well, but I’ll give it up for it – It went OVER three (3) years before failing. It failed April 3, 2019. I remember that because of the event it failed during. I would’ve expected the failure when I transferred the sD card from the S4 to the S8 in May 2018, but the card still worked.

There were no signs of pending failure or issues. The night before (4/2), it worked and I was able to retrieve some photos off of it.

My mother and I went to Knott’s Berry Farm for the Boysenberry Festival. And, any photos take before we left – GONE. No error messages – just gone. I didn’t know until I got home.

What photos I have were the return photos from the drive home. I had briefly glanced at the card data (on my phone) at about 2pm, but after that (without being dropped, banged, over-heated) the card failed. I know some will ask why I didn’t back them up – I was in transit, driving on the freeway, so it wasn’t feasible.

All I know is that my photos were gone. Again, the phone wasn’t dropped, smashed, shocked. Also, no water damage.

So, I had to purchase another sD card for my phone. This time I chose this one – Samsung 32GB 95MB/s (U1) MicroSD EVO Select Memory Card with Adapter (MB-ME32GA/AM).

From April 2019 to the date of this review, it’s been pretty solid. Though I’m not taking any chances. I also store photos to my S8’s internal storage as well as the sD card.

As far as recommending this one – so far it’s working and has been for over five (5) months, so I’ll recommend it for now.

I’ll update the review if things change.
text_fidelity_b: SAMSUNG (MB-ME32GA/AM) 32GB 95MB/s (U1) microSDHC EVO Select Memory Card with Full-Size Adapter

Overall this is a 5-star product and great value!

text_fidelity_a: Linksys LGS308MP Business Poe+ Smart 8 Port Gigabit Network Switch (130W),Black Pretty much a plug and play device; 1 minute to install.  There is supposed to be a configuration program that you can access, but I wasn't able to do so with the IP address given in the instructions.  It wasn't necessary anyway, as the device functions just fine on a simple network without any additional configuration.  There are two things I didn't like about it compared to my old switch, that I was replacing.  First of all, it is a bit larger than my old switch at 8 1/2 inches long compared to my old one that is only 6 1/2 inches.  Also, the power supply is considerably larger at 6 inches long and 3 inches wide and 1 inch thick.  My old switch uses only a large plug that is 1 3/4 x 1 3/4 x 1 1/4.  The second thing I didn't like is that there are no indicator lights to show the functioning ports.  My old switch has lights for each port that is working, which is nice.  You may prefer not to have any lights and if so, this Linksys switch may be to your liking.  Note: there is a disc included with documentation, but I didn't find it to be of any particular use.  On the plus side, this does appear to be a quality, heavy duty switch, so might be well suited for a commercial application (such as in an unattended area, like a computer room in a large business).  It appears to weigh nearly twice what my old switch did, so it is solid.  I have used Linksys products before and found them to be good quality with no issues.  You can buy a cheaper switch that is smaller and does essentially the same thing at a considerably lower price, but you most likely won't get the same quality as you would with this switch.  Also this switch does apparently have a POE (power over internet) feature and if you need that, you also might want to get this.  I don't see a need for POE in my configuration.  Possibly overkill for typical home office, but if you want a good quality switch, it might be worth the extra cost (or not).
text_fidelity_b: Linksys LGS308MP Business Poe+ Smart 8 Port Gigabit Network Switch (130W),Black

10.1 Inch Digital Photo Frame Electronic Picture Frame + 32GB SD Card with Motion Sensor and 1280x800 High Resolution Full IPS LCD 1080P HD Video player/Stereo/MP3/Mp4/Calendar/Alarm/Time/Remote Contr This is the first digital picture frame with which I have worked so I do not have any basis of comparison with others to know if it compares well against other ones or not. That said, it does what it is supposed to do, it does it well and I am happy with it.

Setup is simple and easy. If you have your media ready to go, copy it to the included SD card and pop it in.

On a side note, the card that came with it is 32GB which is huge. That can hold literally thousands of full-resolution images from a digital camera. Assuming that the average high-resolution JPG image is 8mb (which is what comes off my mirrorless camera) it can hold about 4,000 pictures. That all said, this frame can also play back video and sound, so there is more to it than just showing pictures. In that light, the size of the card makes a lot of sense.

The frame is approximately 10” of viewing area. The images are bright and clear which should please most users.

The unit handles a number of audio, video and image formats. The list is not exhaustive, but it does handle the main types in each category.

Included is a little remote. The remote isn’t fancy but it is sufficient for changing settings, moving to the next media element, power on/off, etc.

There’s really only one negative, and that’s the documentation which is written in very poorly-translated English. I would lower my rating of the overall package on this basis except that the product is so self-explanatory and easy to use/understand that the documentation isn’t necessary.

Overall, we are happy with this frame. It works well and it is very easy and straightforward to understand. It handles a lot of formats and can play back audio and video in addition to showing still images.
